If $p$ divides $K$, then $p^{s_p}={\bar\omega}+\rho_p$, where $s_p\geq 2$ and
$1 \le \rho_p\le d$. Since $M={\bar\omega}+d$ is a prime by \cref{lem:s7-prime-M}, $\rho_p\neq d$.                                                                                                                    
Therefore, $1\le \rho_p\le d-1$.
Substituting $\bar{\omega}=p^{s_p}-\rho_p$ into \cref{cor:eq_dK} gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dL_equation}
dK=(d-1)p^{s_p}-\bigl((d-1)\rho_p-1\bigr).
\end{equation}
\cref{cor:eq_dK} also implies that $dK\equiv1\pmod{d-1}$, and hence $\gcd(K,d-1)=1$.
Since $p$ divides $K$ and $K$ is squarefree we also have that
$$
\gcd\bigl(K,(d-1)\rho_p-1\bigr) =\gcd\bigl(K,(d-1)p^{s_p}\bigr) =\gcd(K,p^{s_p})=p.
$$
Since $1\le \rho_p\le d-1$, it follows that the positive integer $(d-1)\rho_p-1$ is at
most $(d-1)^2-1$, and hence its prime divisor $p$ is smaller than $(d-1)^2$.

                                                                                        
                                                                               
By \cref{eq:Qk} and \cref{lem:s7-two-masses}, we have
$$
\frac1{s_2 {\cal Q}_{\cal V}}\le1-\mathbb{S}_K <\frac{2.032}{(d-1)\log M}.
$$
The localized interval implies that $s_2\log2\le\log M$, and after rearranging we have
$$
d-1<\frac{2.032 s_2 {\cal Q}_{\cal V}}{\log M} \le\frac{2.032 {\cal Q}_{\cal V}}{\log2}.
$$
Taking logarithms we get
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:s7-denominator}
    \log(d-1)<\log {\cal Q}_{\cal V}+\log\frac{2.032}{\log2}.
\end{equation}
Finally, if all members in ${\cal V}$ are at most $s_\varnothing$, their pairwise coprimality implies
that ${\cal Q}_{\cal V}$ divides $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,s_\varnothing)$.
Therefore \cref{eq:s7-denominator} and \cref{prop:s7-RS-psi} implies \cref{eq:s7-D-cap}.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:s7-exponent-cap}
Every $v\in{\cal V}$ satisfies $v\le5040$.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:s7-moving}
v<\frac{2520\log \bar{\omega}}{\log \bar{\omega}-\log(d-1)-0.001},  \qquad v\in{\cal V}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Let $p$ be an odd prime divisor of $K$. Since $M$ is a prime,                                           
we have that $\bar{\omega} < 2^{s_2},p^{s_p} < M$.
Let $\Lambda=s_2 \log2-s_p \log p$. Recalling that $(d-1)^2< \bar{\omega}$ and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:s7-Lambda-upper}
0<|\Lambda|=\left|\log\frac{2^{s_2}}{p^{s_p}}\right|\le \log\frac{M-1}{{\bar\omega}}=
\log\bigl(1+\frac{d-1}{{\bar\omega}}\bigr)< \frac{d-1}{{\bar\omega}}< \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\omega}}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $(d-1)^2< \bar{\omega}$ implies that $d^2<2{\bar\omega}$ and therefore \cref{prop:no1large} yields that $\log(1+d/{\bar\omega})<\log(1+2/\sqrt{\bar\omega})<0.001$. By applying the proof of \cref{lem:section5-general-cap}
with $\Lambda=s_2 \log2-s_p \log p$ and $\eta_1<0.001$ gives
$$
s_p< 5040+\frac{0.001}{\log 2}< 5041.
$$
As $s_p$ is an integer, we have that $s_p\le5040$, as required.

Applying the bound $|\Lambda|<(d-1)/{\bar\omega}$ to the proof of \cref{lem:section5-general-cap},
and then $\log {\bar\omega}<2520\log p+ \log(d-1)$, gives
$$
s_p<\frac{\log {\bar\omega}+0.001}{\log p}< 2520+ \frac{\log(d-1)+0.001}{\log p}< 2520+ \frac{\log(d-1)+0.001}{\log \bar{\omega}}s_p,
$$
where the last inequality comes from the localization $p^{s_p}>{\bar\omega}$.
Hence, $s_p<\frac{2520\log \bar{\omega}}{\log \bar{\omega}-\log(d-1)-0.001}$.
This proves \cref{eq:s7-moving}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lm:rangV}
If  $\bar{\omega}\geq \exp(125000)$, then $v\in{\cal V}$ satisfies $24\le v\le 2600$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Denote $x \triangleq 125000$. Then $x \le\log {\bar\omega}$.
                                                                                                                                              
                                                                            
If there exists $d_0$ such that $\log(d-1)<d_0<x$, then \cref{eq:s7-moving} gives
                                                     
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:addeq}
v<\frac{2520\log \bar{\omega}}{\log \bar{\omega} -d_0-0.001} \le\frac{2520x}{x-d_0-0.001}.
\end{equation}
The second inequality holds since $2520x/(x-d_0-0.001)$ is decreasing with $x$ increasing.

Now we start from the initial bound $v\le 5040$ for $v\in\mathcal V$ in \cref{lem:s7-exponent-cap}.
Then  \cref{lem:s7-constraints}
implies the following upper bound on $\log(d-1)$:
$$
\log(d-1) <1.03883\cdot 5040+1.076< 5237.
$$
Taking $d_0=5237<x$ in \cref{eq:addeq} yields
$$
v< \frac{2520\cdot125000}{125000-5237-0.001}< 2631
$$for $v\in\mathcal V$.
We iteratively obtain the second upper bound of $\log(d-1)$:
$$
\log(d-1) <1.03883\cdot 2630+1.076< 2734.
$$
This yields now that
$$
v< \frac{2520\cdot125000}{125000-2734-0.001}< 2577\leq 2600,
$$
and hence $\log(d-1) <1.03883\cdot 2577+1.076< 2679$.

For the lower bound, since $v=s_p$ is a localized exponent for some prime divisor $p$ of $K$, the localized interval implies that $s_p \log p>\log \bar{\omega}$.
                                                          
\cref{lem:s7-constraints}
implies that $\log p<2\log(d-1)$. Therefore,
$$
v=s_p>\frac{\log {\bar\omega}}{2\log(d-1)} >\frac{125000}{2\cdot2679} > 23.
$$
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:s7-large}
If a $1$-perfect code exists in $\textup{J}(n,w)$, then $\bar{\omega}<\exp(125000)$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Suppose that $\log {\bar\omega}\ge x \triangleq 125000$. \cref{lem:lbsv} implies that $\mathbb{S}_{\cal V}>0.9999$
for $\log {\bar\omega}\ge x$. So it suffices to show that $\mathbb{S}_{\cal V}<0.999$.
By \cref{lm:rangV}, ${\cal V}\subseteq[24,2600]\cap\mathbb Z$ and its members are pairwise coprime. We prove that $\mathbb{S}_{\cal V}<0.999$ as follows.


For each prime $p$, define
$$
b_p=\frac1{24}\text{ when }  p\in \{2,3\}, \qquad b_p=\frac{1}{p^2} \text{ when }  p\in \{5,7,11,13,17,19,23\},\qquad
b_p=\frac{1}{p} \text{~when~}  p\ge29.
$$
For every integer $v\in {\cal V}$, we claim that
$$
\frac{1}{v}\le\sum_{p\mid v}b_p.
$$
If $2$ or $3$ divides $v$, then the claim follows since $v \geq 24$ and hence $1/v\le1/24 =b_2=b_3$.
If a prime $p \geq 29$ divides~$v$, then $v \geq p$ and hence $1/v\le1/p=b_p$,
so again a single weight suffices. Otherwise, every prime divisor belongs to $\{5,7,11,13,17,19,23\}$.
If there is only one such prime $p$, then since $v \geq 24 >p$, it follows that $v$ is a power of $p$ and hence $v \geq p^2$
which implies that $1/v \leq 1/{p^2}=b_p$.
If there are two distinct prime divisors $p,q$, then since $pq$ divides $v$ we have
$$
b_p+b_q=\frac{1}{p^2}+\frac{1}{q^2}  \ge\frac{2}{pq}\ge\frac{1}{v},
$$
and the claim is proved.

Now let ${\cal Q}=\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\}$. By the coprimality of the integers in ${\cal V}$, each prime occurs at most once when
we sum over $v\in{\cal V}$, and no prime divisor exceeds $2600$. As a consequence we have that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:RCfore1}
\mathbb{S}_{\cal V}=\sum_{v\in{\cal V}}\frac{1}{v}  \le\sum_{\substack{29\le p\le2600\\p\text{ prime}}}\frac{1}{p}
     +\frac1{12}+\sum_{p\in\mathcal Q\setminus\{2,3\}}\frac{1}{p^2}.
\end{equation}
Apply the upper bound in \cref{prop:quoted-RS-reciprocal} at $x=2600$. As a result, the right side of \cref{eq:RCfore1} is smaller than
$$
\log\log2600+0.2615+\frac1{2\log^2 2600} -\sum_{p\in\mathcal Q}\frac{1}{p}+\frac1{12}+\sum_{p\in\mathcal Q\setminus\{2,3\}}\frac1{p^2} <0.999.
$$Thus $\mathbb{S}_{\cal V}<0.999$ and we finish the proof.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:s7-certificate}
For every integer $250\le u\le180338$ and every odd prime $p\le173$, there is no odd integer $m \ge 3$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:s7-finite-gap}
0<|2^u-m^p|^2<\min\{2^u,m^p\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Suppose that the forbidden  $m$ exists for some $u$ and odd prime $p$. Then
                                              
$$
|2^u-m^p|<2^{u/2},\qquad  m^p>2^u-2^{u/2}>2^{u-1}.
$$
 Let $r=2^{u/p}$. Then both $r$ and $m$ are therefore greater than $2^{(u-1)/p}$. The mean-value theorem yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:s7-root-distance}
|r-m|<\frac{|r^p-m^p|}{p\,2^{(u-1)(p-1)/p}}= \frac{|2^u-m^p|}{p\,2^{(u-1)(p-1)/p}}<
\frac{2^{u/2}}{p\,2^{(u-1)(p-1)/p}}  <2^{-u(1/2-1/p)}<2^{-40},
\end{equation}
where the last inequality is due to $p \geq 3$ and $u \geq 250$. Hence, any forbidden
pair $(p,u)$ would make $r$ lie within $2^{-40}$ of an odd integer. However, if we
compute $r=2^{u/p}$ directly using floating-point arithmetic to guarantee $40$ bits of binary precision, the rounding error cannot be strictly controlled.

To avoid floating-point approximation, we write $r=\sum_{i=-\infty}^{+\infty} r_i2^i$. Then $\lfloor r\rfloor=\sum_{i=0}^{+\infty} r_i2^i$.  \cref{eq:s7-root-distance} forces that the first $40$ fractional bits  $r_i$, $i=-1,-2,\ldots,-40$, are either all zero or all one (i.e, just above or just below an integer), and we need to show that it is impossible. We compute these $40$ bits of $r$ exactly by using pure integer arithmetic as follows.
                                                  
Let $u=pk+\theta$, where $0\le \theta<p$, then $r=2^k\cdot 2^{\theta/p}$.
If $\theta=0$, then $r=2^k$ is an even integer and \cref{eq:s7-root-distance} cannot hold. We may therefore restrict ourselves to $1 \leq \theta<p$.
For each such pair $(p,\theta)$, let
$$
 A_{p,\theta}=\left\lfloor2^{K+\theta/p}\right\rfloor= \left\lfloor2^{K-k}\cdot r \right\rfloor=\sum_{i=0}^{+\infty} r_{i-(K-k)}2^i.
                                                            
$$
                                                                                                        
                                                                                  
Let $K=\left\lfloor\frac{180338}{p}\right\rfloor+41$,
                                   
so $K-k-40\ge1$.                                                             
                                                  
Then
$$
 \left\lfloor2^{40}r\right\rfloor=\sum_{i=0}^{+\infty} r_{i-40}2^i =\left\lfloor\frac{A_{p,\theta}}{2^{K-k-40}}\right\rfloor.
$$
Let $\sigma$ be the residue of this integer modulo $2^{40}$. Equivalently, $\sigma=\lfloor2^{40}\{r\}\rfloor=\sum_{i=0}^{39} r_{i-40}2^i$,
where $\{r\}$ is the fractional part of $r$. Hence,                                  
$\sigma/2^{40}\le\{r\}<(\sigma+1)/2^{40}$.                                                                     
If $1\le \sigma\le2^{40}-2$, then $\{r\}\in[2^{-40},1-2^{-40})$. The distance from $r$ to every integer is at least $2^{-40}$, contradicting \eqref{eq:s7-root-distance}. It is therefore sufficient to check that neither residue $\sigma=0$ nor $\sigma=2^{40}-1$ occurs.

A program explained in (a citation of some link) performs exactly this check.                                                                             
 For each pair $(p,u)$, get a pair $(p,\theta)$ with $\theta\equiv u\pmod p$. If $\theta=0$, then done.                                            
If $\theta\neq 0$, it computes $A_{p,\theta}$ with integer
arithmetic and independently verifies the root enclosure
$$
A_{p,\theta}^{\,p}<2^{pK+\theta}<(A_{p,\theta}+1)^p,
$$ which holds since $A_{p,\theta}=\left\lfloor\left(2^{pK+\theta}\right)^{1/p}\right\rfloor.$
The inequalities are strict because $\theta\neq 0$.                                  
Note that each integer root  $A_{p,\theta}$ will handle every $u\equiv \theta \pmod p$.  It then obtains $\sigma$ by an integer shift of $A_{p,\theta}$ and a modulo operation.
The complete run checks $39(180338-250+1)=7\,023\,471$
pairs $(p, u)$, of which $255\,257$ have $\theta=0$.
Every remaining pair has $1\le \sigma \le2^{40}-2$. The number of pairs $(p,\theta)$ for the computation of the integer roots $A_{p, \theta}$ is only
$\sum_{\substack{3\le p\le173\\p\text{ prime}}}(p-1)=3046$.
                                                                                                              
                                                 
These checks prove the assertion of the certificate;
no floating-point approximation is used.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{prop:s7-bounded}
If there exists a $1$-perfect code in $\textup{J}(n,w)$, where $n>2^{250}$, then $s_2 > 180338$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Assume for contradiction that there exists a $1$-perfect code in J$(n,w)$ and $s_2 \le180338$.
Further,  $s_2 \ge 250$ since $2^{s_2}>\bar{\omega} \ge 2^{249}$ which is obtained from \cref{prop:no1large}.
We provide an upper bound on $\mathbb{S}_{\cal V}$ by splitting its exponents according to their parity.
At most one $v\in{\cal V}$ is even, since two even exponents would not be coprime.
If there exists such $v \in {\cal V}$, then its contribution to $\mathbb{S}_{\cal V}$, $1/v$ is at most $1/2$.

For every odd $v\in\mathcal V$, let $q_v$ be smallest prime divisor of $v$. If $v=s_p$ for the odd prime $p\mid K$,
then let $m=p^{v/q_v}$. Clearly, $m \geq 3$, and $m^{q_v}=p^v$. The two distinct powers $2^{s_2},p^{s_p}$ are contained in $(\bar{\omega},M)$, and hence
$$
0<|2^{s_2} - m^{q_v}|^2   \le(d-1)^2<\bar{\omega}<\min\{2^{s_2},m^{q_v}\}.
$$
Hence, \cref{lem:s7-certificate} rules out $q_v\le173$. On the other hand, \cref{lem:s7-exponent-cap} yields $q_v\le s_p\le5040$.
Distinct odd localized exponents have distinct chosen primes $q_v$,
because the localized exponents are pairwise coprime and also $1/v\le1/q_v$. Summing these bounds yields
$$
\mathbb{S}_{\cal V} \le\frac{1}{2}+\sum_{\substack{173<p\le5040\\p\text{ prime}}}\frac{1}{p} <\frac{1}{2}+\frac{489}{1000}=0.989.
$$
Here, the upper bound $489/1000$ in the second inequality is obtained by a computer program  which adds the reciprocals as exact rational numbers and compares their
sum with $489/1000$ by integer arithmetic.  The upper bound contradicts the lower bound $\mathbb{S}_{\cal V}>0.995$ in \cref{lem:lbsv}, and therefore $s_2 > 180338$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:no-one-perfect-codes-optimized}
There are no $1$-perfect codes in $\textup{J}(n,w)$.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:s7-large}, $\log \bar{\omega}<125000$. The localization  $2^{s_2}<M$ gives
$$
s_2 \log2<\log M=\log(\bar{\omega}+d)<\log \bar{\omega} +1<125001<180339\log2.
$$
As a consequence we have that $s_2 \leq 180338$, contradicting \cref{prop:s7-bounded}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{thm:convergent}
If $p_n$ and $q_n$ are defined by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:convergent}
\begin{aligned}
&  p_0=a_0, ~p_1=a_1a_0+1,~ p_n=a_np_{n-1}+p_{n-2} ~(n\ge 2);\\
&  q_0=1,  ~~q_1=a_1,~~~~~~~~~ q_n=a_nq_{n-1}+q_{n-2} ~(n\ge 2),
\end{aligned}
                                                
                                      
\end{equation}
then \[[a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_n]=\frac{p_n}{q_n}.\]
Further $q_n\geq q_{n-1}>0$ for $n\geq 1$.
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{thm:quoted-legendre}
Let $z$ be real and let $\frac{x}{y}$ be a reduced rational number with $y\geq 1$.
If
\[
\left|\frac{x}{y}-z\right|<\frac1{2y^2},
\]
then \(x/y\) is a convergent of the simple continued fraction of $z$.
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{prop:quoted-etzion-radius2}
If ${n\le40000}$, then there are no $2$-perfect codes in $\textup{J}(n,w)$.
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:section5-two}
There is no $2$-perfect code in any Johnson scheme.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
For $e=2$, \cref{eq-congruence-e+2} implies that $w$ and $\bar{\omega}$ are both even, and \cref{prop:four_divide} implies that
$4\mid(w-1)(w-2)$ and $4\mid({\bar\omega}-1)(\bar{\omega}-2)$. Hence, $w\equiv {\bar\omega}\equiv2\pmod4$.
Hence,
$$
\Phi_2 (n,w)=1+w{\bar\omega}+\binom w2\binom {\bar\omega}2\equiv1+0+1\equiv0\pmod2.
$$
\cref{thm:modulo-p-criterion} with $(p,P,\gamma)=(3,3,1)$ also gives $3\mid\Phi_2(n,w)$. Hence $2,3\mid\Phi_2(n,w)$.  Choose localized powers
$$
{\bar\omega}<2^u,3^v\le {\bar\omega}+d.
$$
By \cref{prop:quoted-etzion-radius2}, no $2$-perfect code exists for $n\le40000$; hence we assume ${\bar\omega}\ge n/2>20000$, so $v\ge10$.                                                                                      
For the upper side, \cref{lem:section5-general-cap} gives $v<15000$.

We next apply the continued fraction argument to give possible values of $u/v$ as follows.
Since ${3^v\le M<2{\bar\omega}}$, we have ${\bar\omega}>3^v/2$ and hence by $|\Lambda|<2/\sqrt {\bar\omega}$ from \cref{eq:section5-Lambda-upper},
\begin{equation}
                                 
\left|\frac{\log3}{\log2}-\frac uv\right|= \frac{|\Lambda|}{v\log2}<\frac{2}{v\log2\cdot\sqrt {\bar\omega}} <\frac{2\sqrt2}{v\log2\cdot3^{v/2}}.
\end{equation}
Since $v\ge 10$ and the function $3^{v/2}/v$ is increasing for $v\ge2$, we have $4\sqrt2v<\log 2\cdot 3^{v/2}$. Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:section5-Legendre-two}
\left|\frac{\log3}{\log2}-\frac{u}{v}\right|<\frac{1}{2v^2}.
\end{equation}
Suppose that $\gcd(u,v)=g\geq 1$, $u=ag$ and $v=bg$. Then $\frac uv=\frac{x}{y}$ with $\frac{x}{y}$ being a reduced fraction. Then \cref{eq:section5-Legendre-two} implies that
$$
\left|\frac{\log3}{\log2}-\frac{x}{y}\right|<\frac{1}{2v^2}\leq\frac{1}{2y^2}.
$$
Applying Legendre's criterion  in \cref{thm:quoted-legendre} with $z=\frac{\log3}{\log2}$ and $\frac{x}{y}$,
we get that $\frac{x}{y}$ is a convergent of $\frac{\log3}{\log2}$. Since $\frac{x}{y}= \frac uv$ and $v<15000$,
$\frac{x}{y}$ can only be some convergent with denominator lying below $15000$.
By the continued fraction algorithm in \eqref{eq:sequence0}, \eqref{eq:sequence1}, \eqref{eq:sequence2},
the required  prefix of the simple continued fraction of $\frac{\log3}{\log2}$ is
$$
\frac{\log3}{\log2}=[1;1,1,2,2,3,1,5,2,23,\ldots].
$$
By \cref{thm:convergent},  the positive convergents whose denominators
lie below $15000$ are $\frac{p_i}{q_i}$ with $i=0,1,2,\ldots, 8$, which are collected in
$$
D=\{1/1,\ 2/1,\ 3/2,\ 8/5,\ 19/12,\ 65/41,\ 84/53,\ 485/306,\ 1054/665\}.
$$
These are all the required convergents since $q_9=15601>15000$ and $q_n\geq q_{n-1}$ (\cref{thm:convergent}).
That is, $u/v$ must belong to $D$.

Finally, we show that $u/v$ cannot equal any one in $D$. Observe that
$$
R_{u,v} \triangleq \frac{|2^u-3^v|^2}{4\min\{2^u,3^v\}}< \frac{d^2}{4\bar{\omega}}\leq \frac{4w}{4\bar{\omega}}\leq 1.
$$
If $u/v=x/y$ for some displayed convergent $x/y$ in $D$, we will show that $R_{u,v}>1$ and thus a contradiction.
Suppose that $\gcd(u,v)=g\geq 1$, $u=xg$ and $v=yg$. Observe that $2^u<3^v$ if and only if $2^x<3^y$. If $2^x<3^y$,
replace $u,v$ by $xg$ and $yg$ in $R_{u,v}$ and consider it as a function of $g$ defined by $x$ and $y$,
$$
R_{x,y}(g):=\frac{(3^{yg}-2^{xg})^2}{4\cdot 2^{xg}}=\frac{2^{xg}}{4}\left(\left(\frac{3^y}{2^x}\right)^g-1\right)^2;
$$
if $2^x>3^y$, just interchange $2^x$ and $3^y$.                                           
Since $R_{x,y}(g)$ is strictly increasing in $g\ge1$, it suffices to compute the
values of $R_{x,y}(g)=R_{u,v}$ for the least integer $g$ such that $v=yg\ge10$. For each $x/y\in D$, the corresponding least
integer $g$ satisfying $yg\ge 10$ are  $g=10,10,5,2,1,1,1,1,1$ and the corresponding pair $(u,v)$ are in
$$
D'=\{(10,10),(20, 10),(15,10),(16,10),(19, 12),(65,41),(84,53),(485,306),(1054,665)\}.
$$
Direct substitution gives $R_{u,v}>1$ for each of these $(u,v)\in D'$ (in fact much bigger than 1).  This contradiction excludes $e=2$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:compPrimesSmall}
If $e \in \{9,10,12,16\}$ and there exists an $e$-perfect code in $\textup{J}(n,w)$, then the following
primes divide $\Phi_e(n,w)$:
\newline
$5,11$ for $e=9$;~~~$11,13$ for $e=10$;~~~$2,7,13$ for $e=12$;~~~$3,17,19$ for $e=16$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
All these primes that divide $\Phi_e(n,w)$ are easily obtained by \cref{thm:modulo-p-criterion}.

The parameters required for the proof $(p,P,\gamma)$ (as defined in \cref{thm:modulo-p-criterion}) and the primes that divide $\Phi_e(n,w)$
as given in the lemma are the triples presented in the following table:
$$
\begin{array}{c|c}
9&(5,5,1),(11,11,2)\\
10&(11,11,1),(13,13,3)\\
12&(2,16,4),(7,7,2),(13,13,1)\\
16&(3,9,2),(17,17,1),(19,19,3).
\end{array}
$$
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:w_g_w4}
If $e\in\{2,9,10,12,16\}$ and there exists an $e$-perfect code in $\textup{J}(n,w)$, then $w>e^4$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:lower bound of w} we have $w>16=2^4$ when $e=2$.

For $e \in \{9,10,12,16\}$ suppose for contradiction that $w\le e^4$. By \cref{eq:section5-w-over-z} and since $d\le e\sqrt w$, we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:section5-quartic-basic-upperSwcond}
\bar{\omega}<e^4+e^3,\qquad M=\bar{\omega} +d<e^4+2e^3.
\end{equation}

For $e=9$, \cref{lem:compPrimesSmall} yields prime divisors $5$ and $11$,
and by \cref{prop:lower bound of w} we have that $\bar{\omega} > 199$ which is larger than $11^2$ and $5^3$.
By \cref{eq:section5-quartic-basic-upperSwcond} we have that $M<8019<11^4$ and therefore the localized exponent of $11$ is $3$ and hence
$\bar{\omega}<1331$. Therefore $M=\bar{\omega}+d<1331+9\sqrt{1331}<1660<5^5$.
This implies that the localized exponent of $5$ is consequently $4$, and hence $\bar{\omega}<625$.
Therefore, $11^3$ and $5^4$  are contained in the localized interval $(\bar{\omega},\bar{\omega}+d]$, and it implies that
$$
706=11^3-5^4<d\le9\sqrt {\bar\omega}<9\sqrt{625}=225,
$$
a contradiction, and thus $w > 9^4$.

For $e=10$, \cref{lem:compPrimesSmall} yields the prime divisors $11$, and $13$,
and by \cref{prop:lower bound of w} we have that $\bar{\omega}> 241$ which is larger than $13^2$ and $11^2$.
By \cref{eq:section5-quartic-basic-upperSwcond} we have that $M<12000<11^4 <13^4$ and therefore the localized exponent of $11$ is $3$
and the localized exponent of $13$ is $3$.
In particular $\bar{\omega} <11^3=1331$, and hence
$$
866=13^3-11^3<d\le10\sqrt {\bar\omega}<10\sqrt{1331}<365,
$$
a contradiction, and thus $w > 10^4$.

For $e=12$, \cref{lem:compPrimesSmall} yields the prime divisors $2,7$, and $13$,
and by \cref{prop:lower bound of w} we have that $\bar{\omega}> 337$ which is larger than $13^2$.
By \cref{eq:section5-quartic-basic-upperSwcond} we have that $M<24192<13^4$, and therefore the localized exponent
of $13$ is $3$. In particular $\bar{\omega} <13^3=2197 \leq M$, and hence
$$
M=\bar{\omega}+d<{\bar\omega}+12\sqrt {\bar\omega}<2197+12\sqrt{2197}<2760.
$$
Since $M<2760$ which is smaller than $7^5$ and $2^{12}$ and ${\bar\omega}=M-d> 13^3-12\sqrt{2197}>1634 > 2^{10}>7^3$,
it follows that the localized exponent of $7$ is $4$ and the localized exponent of $2$ is $11$. As a consequence
$$
\bar{\omega}<2048,\qquad {\bar\omega}=M-d>7^4-12\sqrt{2048}>1857.
$$
We now use the residue localization already contained in \cref{lem:residue-localization}. For the three
parameters $(p,P,\gamma)=(13,13,1),(7,7,2),(2,16,4)$ given by \cref{thm:modulo-p-criterion},
$$
w,\bar{\omega}\equiv12\pmod{13},\qquad w,\bar{\omega} \equiv4\text{ or }5\pmod7,\qquad w,{\bar\omega}\equiv9,10,11,\text{ or }12\pmod{16}.
$$
\cref{eq-congruence-e+2} with $e+2=14$ sharpens the congruence modulo $7$ to $w\equiv \bar{\omega} \equiv5\pmod7$.
A simple calculation gives the possible residues modulo $13\cdot7\cdot16=1456$. Writing $w\text{ or }{\bar\omega}=12+13r$,
the congruence modulo $7$ gives $r\equiv0\pmod7$, while the congruence modulo $16$ gives $r\equiv0,1,6,11\pmod{16}$.
Combining these modulo $7\cdot16=112$ yields
$$
r\equiv0,49,70,91\pmod{112},
$$
and hence
$$
w,{\bar\omega}\pmod{1456}\in\{12,649,922,1195\}.
$$
None of these residue classes has a representative in $1857<{\bar\omega}<2048$, a contradiction and thus $w > 12^4$.

For $e=16$, \cref{lem:compPrimesSmall} yields the prime divisors $17$ and $19$,
and by \cref{prop:lower bound of w} we have that $\bar{\omega} > 577$ which is larger than $19^2$ and $17^2$.
By \cref{eq:section5-quartic-basic-upperSwcond} we have that $M<73728<17^4 <19^4$ and therefore the localized exponent $17$ is $3$
and the localized exponent of $19$ is $3$. In particular $\bar{\omega} <17^3=4913$, and hence
\[
19^3-17^3=1946<d\le16\sqrt {\bar{\omega}}<16\sqrt{4913}<1122,
\]
a contradiction, and thus $w > 16^4$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:section5-exponent-packing}
Let ${\cal E}$ be a set of integers such that $3 \leq u \leq N$ for every $u \in {\cal E}$,
and $\gcd(u,v)\le2$ whenever $u$ and $v$ are distinct integers in ${\cal E}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:section5-pack-gcd2}
\sum_{u\in{\cal E}}\frac{1}{u}\le\frac{1}{4}+\sum_{\substack{3\le v\le N\\v\text{ prime}}}\frac{1}{v}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
For $u\in{\cal E}$, put $m_u=u$ when $u$ is odd and $m_u=u/2$ when $u$ is even. Hence, $m_u\ge 2$ since $u\ge 3$.
Since $\gcd(u,v)\le2$, it follows that $\gcd(m_u,m_v)=1$,
which implies that at most one $m_u$ is even. Equivalently, at most one $u \in {\cal E}$ is divisible by $4$, and it contributes at most $1/4$ to the left sum.
For every remaining $m_u$, choose an odd prime divisor $r_u\mid m_u$. Since the numbers $m_u$ are pairwise
coprime, it follows that the $r_u$s are distinct primes,
and $r_u\le m_u\le u\le N$. Since $1/u\le1/r_u$, we have \cref{eq:section5-pack-gcd2}.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:section5-small-unified}
There is no $e$-perfect code in the Johnson scheme for $e\in\{9,10,12,16\}$.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Assume that there exists an $e$-perfect code in J$(n,w)$ for some $e\in\{9,10,12,16\}$.
If $c_e=\frac e{e+1}-\frac{1}{e}$ then we have that $d/\bar{\omega}<1/e$. We also have that
$M=\bar{\omega}+d<\bar{\omega}(1+1/e)$, and $w-h_i>w-d>c_e{\bar\omega}$ with $h_i$ defined in
\cref{thm:section5-Lloyd-factorization}. Lloyd's theorem also implies that
$\Phi_e(n,w)>(c_e{\bar{\omega}}^2)^e/(e!)^2$, and therefore
$$
\log\Phi_e>2e\log {\bar\omega}+e\log c_e-2\log(e!).
$$

Using \cref{lem:section5-Lloyd-mass} with $\log M<\log \bar{\omega}+\log(1+1/e)$ we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:section5-small-lower-unified}
\mathbb{S}-e \ge \frac{\log\Phi_e}{\log M}-e> \frac{e\log {\bar\omega}+e\log c_e-2\log(e!)-e\log(1+1/e)}{\log {\bar\omega}+\log(1+1/e)}.
\end{equation}
The right side increases with $\log {\bar\omega}$, because its derivative (with $\log \bar{\omega}$ as its parameter)
has numerator $2e\log(1+1/e)-e\log c_e+2\log(e!)>0$. We may therefore replace $\bar{\omega}$ by $e^4$ in this lower bound,
keep the inequality and have a lower bound on $\mathbb{S}-e$.

To obtain an upper bound on $\mathbb{S}-e$, we first bound the remaining localized exponent classes. If $p,q$ are distinct odd prime
divisors of $\Phi_e(n,w)$ and $g=\gcd(s_p,s_q)\ge 3$, then let $p^{s_p}=x^g$ and $q^{s_q}=y^g$.
Since $x,y$ are distinct odd integers, we have that $|x-y|\ge2$, and the mean-value theorem implies that
$$
|x^g-y^g|>2g {\bar\omega}^{(g-1)/g}\geq 6{\bar\omega}^{2/3}.
$$
For each $e\in\{9,10,12,16\}$, one has $6e^{2/3}>e$, and hence $\bar{\omega}>e^4$ implies that
$6{\bar\omega}^{2/3}>6e^{2/3}\sqrt {\bar\omega}>e\sqrt {\bar\omega}\ge d$, contradicting the length of the localized interval. Therefore,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:section5-small-gcd2}
\gcd(s_p,s_q)\le2
\end{equation}
for distinct odd prime divisors $p$ and $q$ of $\Phi_e(n,w)$.

Let $N_2$ be the number of odd prime divisors with localized exponent $2$.
If their bases are $p_1<\cdots<p_{N_2}$, then the mean-value theorem yields
$$
p_{j+1}^2-p_j^2>4p_j>4\sqrt{\bar{\omega}}.
$$
Summing over all $p_{j+1}^2-p_j^2$ in the localized interval gives $4(N_2-1)\sqrt {\bar\omega}<d\le e\sqrt {\bar\omega}$, so the contribution
of these localized exponents is $N_2/2$ which is less than $1/2+e/8$.

For odd-prime exponents $s_p\ge3$, \cref{lem:section5-general-cap} implies that $s_p<15000$.
Now we can apply \cref{eq:section5-small-gcd2}, \cref{lem:section5-exponent-packing}, and \cref{eq:section5-Dusart-simple}.
The primes chosen in the proof of \cref{lem:section5-exponent-packing} are odd, so the term $1/2$ belonging to the prime $2$ may be removed from \cref{eq:section5-Dusart-simple}. As a consequence we have that
$$
\sum_{\substack{p\mid\Phi_e(n,w)\\p\text{ odd},\ s_p\ge3}} \hspace{-0.3cm}\frac1{s_p}<\frac14+\left(\log\log15000+0.278-\frac12\right)=\log\log15000+0.028<2.292.
$$
If $2$ divides $\Phi_e(n,w)$, then the contribution implied by $2^{s_2}>\bar{\omega}$ is $1/s_2<\log2/\log \bar{\omega}<\log2/(4\log e)$. Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:section5-small-upper-unified}
\mathbb{S}-e<\frac12+\frac e8+2.292+\frac{\log2}{4\log e}.
\end{equation}
Evaluating \eqref{eq:section5-small-lower-unified} at $\bar{\omega}=e^4$ gives
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
e&\text{lower bound for }\mathbb S-e&\text{upper bound from \eqref{eq:section5-small-upper-unified}}\\ \hline
9&>5.66&<4.00\\
10&>6.32&<4.12\\
12&>7.60&<4.37\\
16&>10.13&<4.86.
\end{array}
$$
Each row gives a contradiction, excluding all four radii. Hence, there
is no $e$-perfect code in J$(n,w)$ for each radius $e \in \{9,10,12,16\}$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:section6-weight}
If there exists a $4$-perfect code in $\textup{J}(n,w)$ then $w> 10000$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:lower bound of w} we have $w\ge 50$. The last summand of $\Phi_4 (n,w)$ implies that
$$
\Phi_4 (n,w) \ge\binom{w}{4}\binom{\bar{\omega}}{4}>\frac{(w-2)^8}{576}.
$$
By \cref{eq:Roos} we have that $\bar{\omega} < 5w/4$ and by \cref{cor:str_redund} we have that $d \leq 4 \sqrt{w}$. These two bounds imply that
$$
M=\bar{\omega}+d<(5w)/4+4\sqrt{w}.
$$
For any number $z$ such that $50\le z \le w$, taking logarithms of these inequalities imply that
$$
\log\Phi_4 (n,w)>8\log w+8\log(1-2/z)-\log 576
$$
and
$$
\log M< \log w+\log(5/4+4/\sqrt z).
$$
As a consequence, \cref{lem:section5-Lloyd-mass} implies that
$$
\mathbb{S}\ge \frac{\log\Phi_4(n,w)}{\log M}> \frac{8\log w+8\log(1-2/z)-\log576}{\log w+\log(5/4+4/\sqrt{z})}.
$$
The right side of the inequality increases when $\log w$ increases. Hence,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:section6-R4}
\mathbb{S}>R(z) \triangleq \frac{8\log z+8\log(1-2/z)-\log576}{\log z+\log(5/4+4/\sqrt{z})}.
\end{equation}

Consider now the localized exponents of primes dividing $\Phi_4(n,w)$.
We claim that for each fixed $s\ge2$, at most one odd prime can have localized exponent $s$.
If $p<q$ are odd primes with the same localized exponent $s$, then by the mean-value theorem we have that
$$
q^s-p^s>2s {\bar{\omega}}^{(s-1)/s}\ge4\sqrt {\bar\omega}\ge d,
$$
contradicting the length of the localized interval. Thus, each localized exponent greater than one appears at most once.
We continue with this observation and distinguish between two cases depending whether $w$ is at most $256$ or not.

Suppose first that $50\le w\le256$ which implies that $M<\frac54w+4\sqrt w\le 384<5^4$, while
$\bar{\omega} \ge 50 >5^2$. Hence, the localized exponent of $5$ must be $3$ and
by the definition of the localized interval we have that $\bar{\omega}<5^3=125$,
and therefore $M={\bar\omega}+d<125+4\sqrt{125}<170<7^3$. This implies that every prime
divisor of $\Phi_4(n,w)$ greater than $6$ has localized exponent at most $2$.
Moreover, since it is required that $p^{s_p} \geq 50$, it follows that $s_2\ge 6$ and $s_3\ge 4$  when the prime divides $\Phi_4 (n,w)$. Hence,
$$
\mathbb{S} \le 4+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{3}=5.25<5.4593<R(50),
$$
contradicting \eqref{eq:section6-R4}.

Suppose now that $256<w\le10^4$ which implies that $M<\frac54w+4\sqrt w\le12900<7^5$.
Hence, every prime greater than $6$ that divides $\Phi_4(n,w)$ has a localized exponent at most $4$.
Since $\bar{\omega} \ge w>256$, when a prime $2$, $3$, or $5$ divides $\Phi_4(n,w)$, their localized
exponents satisfy $s_2\ge9$, $s_3\ge6$, and $s_5\ge4$. Therefore,
$$
S\le4+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\frac19+\frac16+\frac14=\frac{101}{18}<5.612<6.3762<R(256),
$$
contradicting \cref{eq:section6-R4}.

These contradictions imply that $w>10^4$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:no-four-perfect-codes}
There is no $4$-perfect code in any Johnson scheme.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Assume for contradiction that there exists a $4$-perfect code in J$(n,w)$.
By \cref{lem:section6-weight} and \cref{eq:section6-R4} we have that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:section6-mass-lower}
\mathbb S>R(10^4)>7.1130.
\end{equation}
We derive an upper bound on $\mathbb{S}$ to obtain a contradiction.
If distinct odd primes $p,q$, different from $5$, have $g=\gcd(s_p,s_q)\ge2$,
then let $p^{s_p}=x^g$ and $q^{s_q}=y^g$. Since $x,y$ are distinct integers with $|x-y|\ge2$
and $\min\{x,y\}> \bar{\omega}^{1/g}$, then by the mean-value theorem we have
$$
|x^g-y^g|> g \bar{\omega}^{(g-1)/g}|x-y|\ge 4\sqrt {\bar\omega}\ge d,
$$
with a contradiction to the length of the localized interval.
Thus $\gcd(s_p,s_q)=1$, and in particular there is no equal localized exponent greater than one for two prime
divisors of $\Phi_4(n,w)$ with a possible exception for the primes $2$ and $5$.
For each prime $p\notin \{2,5\}$ with exponent $s_p\ge 2$, take a prime~$r_p$ dividing~$s_p$.
This choice of $r_p$ implies that $1/s_p\le 1/r_p$ and two such primes $r_p$ and $r_q$ are distinct since $\gcd(s_p,s_q)=1$.
Also since \cref{lem:section5-general-cap} implies that $s_p<15000$ for $p \notin \{2,5\}$, it follows by
applying \cref{eq:section5-Dusart-simple} that
$$
\sum_{\substack{p\mid\Phi_4\\p\ne2,5,\ s_p\ge2}}\frac1{s_p}\le\sum_{\substack{q<15000\\q\text{ prime}}}\frac1q<\log\log15000+0.278.
$$
Exponent $1$ contributes at most $4$ by \cref{lem:number_mult1}, $2^{s_2}>{\bar\omega}>10^4$ and $5^{s_5}>{\bar\omega}>10^4$ implies
that $1/s_2<\log2/\log(10^4)$ and $1/s_5<\log5/\log(10^4)$.
Summing all the contributions yields
$$
\mathbb{S}<4+\log\log15000+0.278+\log2/\log(10^4)+\log5/\log(10^4)<6.7915,
$$
contradicting \eqref{eq:section6-mass-lower} and therefore there are no $4$-perfect codes in the Johnson scheme.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
